plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs semaglutide (Ozempic) in type 2 diabetes: the SURPASS-2 randomized head-to-head trial (NEJM 2021; adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin; 40 weeks; open-label; tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg arms vs semaglutide 1 mg). Covers A1C, weight, stomach side effects, low blood sugar and stopping rates, what the trial can and can't tell you, and questions to ask your prescriber.
plan.angle: Use the same SURPASS-2 deep-dive, but only after confirming no Mounjaro vs Ozempic long video is live. If one is, make this a clearly distinct A1C-focused piece. Suggested title: 'Mounjaro vs Ozempic in Type 2 Diabetes: What the Head-to-Head Trial Found'. Thumbnail: 'WHICH LOWERED A1C MORE?', subtext 'tirzepatide vs semaglutide 1 mg', no answer stated. Sentence 1: 'If you have type 2 diabetes and take metformin: in a 40-week trial that randomly assigned adults to tirzepatide or semaglutide one milligram, A1C fell more on all three tirzepatide doses.' Emergency card: each drug's Medication Guide sentence verbatim ('Stop using [drug] and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away…', with that guide's exact clause). Follow it with the fixed line 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Low blood sugar: per-arm SURPASS-2 rates. Risk is higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea; the labels also report it in adults without type 2 diabetes. Everything else as planned: open-label and Lilly-funded limits, SURMOUNT-5 as one neutral line about a separate trial, prescriber questions, no dosing, cost or switching talk, and the full 'Not personal advice' and prescriber line.

plan.why:
Playbook queue #2 takes the slot now that Foundayo is parked. It's an approved-drug head-to-head against tirzepatide (our best format) with high search demand for 'mounjaro vs ozempic', and it rests on one peer-reviewed RCT plus the labels, so it should pass the fact-check first time. | fact-check: The core topic holds up. I confirmed SURPASS-2 (Frías et al., NEJM 2021;385:503–515): a 40-week, open-label, randomised trial in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg arms (n≈470 each) against semaglutide 1 mg (n=469). A1C change was −2.01, −2.24 and −2.30 points against −1.86. Tirzepatide was noninferior and superior at all three doses. Extra weight loss against semaglutide was −1.9, −3.6 and −5.5 kg. Lilly funded it. Sentence 1 ('A1C fell more on all three tirzepatide arms') is supported. Approve with these changes:
(1) Duplicate risk. The playbook's linking list already routes 'Mounjaro vs Ozempic → Zepbound vs Wegovy', which suggests a Mounjaro vs Ozempic long video already exists. Check the live list before scripting. If one is live, don't re-produce it. Either reframe this as a distinct SURPASS-2 A1C deep-dive with a clearly different title and thumbnail, or drop it.
(2) Emergency wording. 'Stop… and get medical help right away' is the Foundayo guide's wording. The Mounjaro and Ozempic Medication Guides say 'Stop using [drug] and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away…'. Copy each guide's own sentence, including its exact 'with or without…' clause. Open each guide and find the sentence before writing it. I couldn't read the Mounjaro guide PDF, and a search summary showed 'nausea or vomiting', which conflicts with the craft note's 'with or without vomiting'.
(3) Don't-stop line. Use the fixed line exactly: 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Don't add 'switch' or the plural 'medicines'.
(4) Low blood sugar. Every SURPASS-2 participant had type 2 diabetes. Keep the per-arm rates as printed and the insulin/sulfonylurea line. Attribute 'also reported in adults without type 2 diabetes' to the US labels, not the trial.
(5) Thumbnail. 'WHICH DROPPED MORE?' doesn't name the measure. Use 'WHICH LOWERED A1C MORE?' with 'tirzepatide vs semaglutide 1 mg' as subtext.
(6) Limits chapter. Say the trial tested semaglutide 1 mg only, and say nothing about other doses or rankings. Never call cross-trial numbers head-to-head.
(7) Weight chapter. Frame the figures as trial averages in adults with type 2 diabetes, and keep the paper's measure label: treatment-regimen or efficacy, in plain words.

package.description:
Both Medication Guides (Mounjaro and Ozempic) say to stop using the medicine and call your healthcare provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

In SURPASS-2 (NEJM, 2021), adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin were randomized to tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg or semaglutide 1 mg for 40 weeks. On average, all three tirzepatide doses lowered A1C more than semaglutide 1 mg, with more weight loss, and more people stopping for adverse events. One open-label, Lilly-funded trial: not a forecast for your body.

script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) vs Ozempic: Which Lowered A1C More?
script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity, answer-first (Exp H). Sentence 1 names tirzepatide and semaglutide 1 mg, the population (adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin), the 40-week randomized design and the hedged answer: A1C fell more, on average, on all three tirzepatide doses. The headline numbers follow at about 15–25 s, each with its hedge and unit. Then a one-sentence open loop about stopping rates, which pays off in the 'Who stopped' chapter.

scenes.narration: That's Mounjaro's active ingredient against Ozempic's, in a trial called SURPASS two. On the top tirzepatide dose, A-one-C fell by an estimated two point three percentage points. On semaglutide, it fell by an estimated one point eight six percentage points.

scenes.retention_device: Headline number delivered by about 20 s (second concrete payoff)

scenes.narration: Both groups improved, and in this trial both medicines were once-weekly injections. So the useful questions are how big the gap really is, what it cost in stomach trouble and low blood sugar, and what this trial can't tell you.
scenes.retention_device: Promise: what the viewer will get

scenes.narration: First, the number your clinic checks every few months, and what one point of it actually means.
A-one-C is a blood test that reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the past three months. It's reported as a percentage, so a drop of one point means one whole percentage point.

visual.stock_query: calendar pages flipping, friendly blood drop

scenes.narration: The adults in this trial started at an average A-one-C of eight point two eight percent. Their average age was fifty-six point six years. Imagine someone like Dev, a hypothetical fifty-six-year-old who's been on metformin for years and is stuck right around that number.

visual.stock_query: tired man reading lab results, kitchen

scenes.retention_device: Relatable thread introduced (clearly hypothetical), tied to trial data

scenes.narration: Across one thousand eight hundred seventy-nine adults, split evenly into four groups, the lowest tirzepatide dose, five milligrams, lowered A-one-C by an estimated two point zero one percentage points.
scenes.on_screen_text: Lowest tirzepatide dose: type 2 diabetes + metformin, 40 weeks

visual.stat_label: A1C points: tirzepatide 5 mg vs semaglutide 1 mg

scenes.retention_device: Concrete number with comparator on card

scenes.narration: Ten milligrams lowered it by two point two four. Semaglutide one milligram, as you heard, by one point eight six. So even the lowest tirzepatide dose came out ahead.
scenes.on_screen_text: Even the lowest dose led (type 2 diabetes + metformin, 40 wks)

visual.stat_label: A1C points: tirzepatide 10 mg vs semaglutide 1 mg

scenes.narration: So how big is the gap? On five milligrams, the extra drop was zero point one five points. On ten, zero point three nine. On fifteen, zero point four five. Each one compared with semaglutide.
scenes.on_screen_text: Extra A1C drop vs semaglutide 1 mg
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, answered immediately

scenes.narration: In statistical terms, all three tirzepatide doses were noninferior and superior to semaglutide on A-one-C. In plain words: not worse, and better on average.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not worse, and better on average

scenes.narration: But keep the honest frame. This isn't one medicine working and one failing. Semaglutide lowered A-one-C by an estimated one point eight six percentage points too. Tirzepatide's doses just lowered it further.

visual.fact: Both lowered A1C; tirzepatide lowered it further

scenes.narration: That's the headline. But A-one-C wasn't the only thing that moved, and the next number is probably the one you've heard about at the dinner table.
Weight. These are trial averages in adults with type two diabetes, not a forecast for your body.
The average starting weight was ninety-three point seven kilograms. Over forty weeks, all four groups lost weight, and the tirzepatide groups lost more.
Compared with semaglutide, the extra loss was one point nine kilograms on five milligrams. Three point six on ten. And five point five on fifteen.
scenes.on_screen_text: Estimated extra average loss vs semaglutide 1 mg, 40 wks

scenes.narration: Those are the paper's main estimates. They count everyone as randomly assigned, whether or not they kept taking the trial drug or needed extra diabetes medicine.
If you think in pounds, five and a half kilograms is about twelve pounds more than the semaglutide group lost, on average, on the top dose.

visual.stat_label: Extra loss, tirzepatide 15 mg vs semaglutide 1 mg

scenes.narration: For someone like Dev, that might matter. But weight is one health measure among many, and it wasn't the trial's main goal. A-one-C was.
So far this sounds one-sided. Here's where the trade-offs start.
The stomach. If you've heard the nausea stories, this chapter is for you.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset, speaks to a felt worry

scenes.narration: The paper says the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal, and primarily mild to moderate in severity, in both the tirzepatide and semaglutide groups.
scenes.on_screen_text: Primarily mild to moderate in both groups

scenes.narration: Nausea was reported in seventeen to twenty-two percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on the dose, and eighteen percent on semaglutide.

visual.stat_label: Nausea: tirzepatide 5–15 mg vs semaglutide 1 mg

scenes.narration: Diarrhea: thirteen to sixteen percent, against twelve percent. Vomiting: six to ten percent, against eight percent.
Notice the pattern. For nausea and vomiting, semaglutide's figure sits inside tirzepatide's range. Diarrhea was higher on tirzepatide at every dose.
The Mounjaro label also notes that tirzepatide delays stomach emptying. The delay is largest after the first dose, and this effect diminishes over time.

Stomach effects were among the most common adverse events in this trial. If you feel heavy or queasy, you don't have to just push through. Tell your prescriber; that's exactly what they want to hear about.
scenes.retention_device: Name the feeling and give agency

scenes.narration: The Mounjaro Medication Guide also says diarrhea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, called dehydration, which may cause kidney problems. It says it's important to drink fluids to help reduce your chance of dehydration. That's unless you've been told to limit fluids.

visual.stock_query: glass of water, kidney mascot smiling

scenes.narration: Stomach effects are the trade-off people expect. The next one is the worry that can follow people with diabetes to bed at night.
Low blood sugar. The Mounjaro safety information lists signs like shakiness, sweating and a fast heartbeat.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a felt moment

scenes.narration: In this trial, low blood sugar was counted when blood sugar fell below fifty-four milligrams per deciliter.
On tirzepatide, it was reported in zero point six percent of the five milligram group. Zero point two percent of the ten milligram group. And one point seven percent of the fifteen milligram group.
scenes.retention_device: Per-arm numbers, one at a time

scenes.narration: On semaglutide, it was zero point four percent. Even the highest figure, one point seven percent, is fewer than two people in every hundred.
scenes.on_screen_text: Fewer than 2 in 100 (type 2 diabetes + metformin, 40 wks)

visual.stat_label: Semaglutide 1 mg: blood sugar below 54 mg/dL

scenes.narration: Remember, everyone in this trial had type two diabetes and was taking metformin. The US safety information for both medicines says the risk of low blood sugar may be higher when they're used with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
scenes.on_screen_text: Higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea

scenes.narration: And the Zepbound label, tirzepatide's label for weight management, says low blood sugar has also been associated with tirzepatide and other GLP-1 medicines in adults without type two diabetes.
scenes.on_screen_text: Also linked to low blood sugar without type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: So if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, that's a question for your prescriber, never a reason to change anything on your own.
scenes.retention_device: Agency: what to do with it

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the number I promised at the start. It isn't about blood sugar at all.
Who stopped, and why it's the number I'd bring to an appointment.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset, most surprising section last

scenes.narration: A medicine can only help while you're taking it. So the paper also counted how many people stopped the trial drug because of adverse events.
scenes.retention_device: Why it matters before the number

scenes.narration: On tirzepatide, that was six percent on five milligrams, and eight point five percent on both ten and fifteen milligrams.
scenes.on_screen_text: Stopped for adverse events: tirzepatide, 40 weeks

scenes.narration: On semaglutide one milligram, it was four point one percent.
scenes.on_screen_text: Semaglutide 1 mg: stopped for adverse events (type 2 diabetes + metformin, 40 wks)

visual.stat_label: Semaglutide 1 mg: stopped for adverse events

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. The two higher tirzepatide doses, the ones that lowered A-one-C the most, also had the highest share of people stopping for adverse events.
scenes.on_screen_text: Higher doses: more A1C drop, more stopping

scenes.narration: Serious adverse events were also higher on tirzepatide than on semaglutide, though not in step with the dose. On tirzepatide, five point three to seven percent, depending on the dose. On semaglutide, two point eight percent.

visual.stat_label: Serious adverse events, any tirzepatide dose vs semaglutide 1 mg (type 2 diabetes + metformin, 40 wks)

scenes.narration: Put it together and you get the real picture. On average, tirzepatide brought more A-one-C lowering and more weight loss, with more people stopping for adverse events.
So for Dev, the better question isn't which one is stronger. It's which one he can stay on, with his life, his stomach and his other medicines. That's a conversation, not a scoreboard.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main loop, return to thread

scenes.narration: But before you take any of this into that conversation, you need to know what this trial can't tell you.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop before chapter change

scenes.narration: The limits. Every good trial has them, and this one has three big ones.
One: it was open-label. Participants and investigators knew which drug each person was taking, and that can shape how symptoms get noticed and reported.
Two: it was funded by Eli Lilly, the company that makes tirzepatide. That doesn't make the results wrong, but it's worth knowing who paid.

visual.stock_query: receipt on lab bench, raised eyebrow

scenes.narration: Three: it compared tirzepatide only with semaglutide one milligram. That's the only semaglutide dose this trial can speak to.
scenes.retention_device: Limit that corrects a common assumption

scenes.narration: A separate trial, SURMOUNT five, compared these two medicines for weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, who didn't have diabetes. It asked a different question in different people, so its numbers don't belong in this comparison.
scenes.retention_device: One neutral context line that pre-empts confusion

scenes.narration: And forty weeks is short. The trial was designed around A-one-C in adults already on metformin, not heart attacks, strokes or the long term.
scenes.retention_device: Final limit, sets up the takeaways

scenes.narration: So what do you actually do with all of this? Three takeaways, two safety lines, and you're ready.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, promise of the checklist

scenes.narration: One: in adults on metformin over forty weeks, all three tirzepatide doses lowered A-one-C more, on average, than semaglutide one milligram.
Two: the higher doses also had more people stopping for adverse events, so ask about tolerability, not just the headline.
Three: this is one open-label, Lilly-funded trial against one semaglutide dose. A large randomized trial, with clear edges.

Questions worth bringing: Given my A-one-C and my other medicines, which option fits me? How would we handle stomach effects if they show up? And what's my low blood sugar risk with what I already take?

factcheck.summary:
I checked the script against the SURPASS-2 abstract (NEJM 2021;385:503–515, through Europe PMC). Every number matches: n=1879, starting A1C 8.28%, age 56.6, weight 93.7 kg, A1C change −2.01, −2.24 and −2.30 vs −1.86, differences −0.15, −0.39 and −0.45, weight differences −1.9, −3.6 and −5.5 kg, the nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting ranges, low blood sugar below 54 mg/dL at 0.6%, 0.2% and 1.7% vs 0.4%, and noninferior and superior. The script also correctly says the trial was open-label. Lilly funding isn't stated in the abstract, and I didn't open a page that confirms it. The EU trial register gives serious adverse events of 7.02%, 5.33% and 5.74% vs 2.77%, which matches s43's "5.3 to 7 vs 2.8", including the point that they didn't rise with dose. A search snippet citing Lilly medical-information sources gives stopping for adverse events of 6.0%, 8.5% and 8.5% vs 4.1%, and the script matches it. I didn't open those pages myself.

Label wording checks out on the live pages: the Mounjaro and Ozempic safety lines (s58, s59), the dehydration line (s28) and the low blood sugar signs (s30); Mounjaro PI section 5.3 and the section 12.2 stomach-emptying sentence (s26); and Zepbound PI section 5.7, "associated with … in adults without type 2 diabetes" (s35). The NIDDK A1C wording (s06) and the SURMOUNT-5 citation (s51) are also right.

The live Mounjaro safety page (labels revised 8/2026) now reads "with or without nausea or vomiting". That differs from the older craft note ("with or without vomiting"), so s58 is correct as written and nobody downstream should "fix" it back.

The script answers the title, keeps the hedges, keeps both trials' populations right, mentions side effects in a helpful way, includes the fluid caveat, the don't-stop line and the disclaimer, and clearly presents Dev as hypothetical. There are three small fixes below.

issues.claim: They count everyone as randomly assigned, whether or not they kept taking the trial drug or needed extra diabetes medicine.
issues.problem: The paper's main estimates count everyone who was randomly assigned and got at least one dose, not literally everyone randomized. It's a small overstatement.
issues.fix: Narration: "Those are the paper's main estimates. They count everyone who was randomly assigned and took at least one dose, whether or not they kept taking the trial drug or needed extra diabetes medicine." On-screen text: "Counts everyone who started"

issues.claim: source_ids include S1c (Lilly investor news release)
issues.problem: The rules don't allow newsroom or press-release pages as sources. The SURPASS-2 abstract (S1) already supports everything in s25.
issues.fix: Change s25 source_ids to ["S1"] and delete S1c from the sources list.

issues.claim: ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information: Warnings and Precautions, Hypoglycemia
issues.problem: Source titles must give section numbers. The quoted sentence is in section 5.7 of the 8/2026 PI.
